title: Enteric Fever (Typhoid and Paratyphoid): Diagnosis, Culture-Directed Treatment and Complications (India)

pathophysiology.summary: Systemic infection by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi or Paratyphi A, acquired by faecal-oral transmission through contaminated water or food. Organisms cross the small-bowel mucosa, multiply in Peyer's patches and the reticuloendothelial system, and seed the bloodstream, liver, spleen, bone marrow and gallbladder. Fluoroquinolone resistance in India is high (ICMR 2019 reports up to 69% for S. Typhi and 23% for S. Paratyphi A), so empirical ciprofloxacin is no longer reliable.
keyMechanisms: Invasion through M cells overlying Peyer's patches, with intracellular survival inside macrophages that carry bacteria to mesenteric nodes, liver, spleen and bone marrow.
Sustained bacteraemia and cytokine release cause the step-ladder fever, malaise, relative bradycardia and hepatosplenomegaly.
Hyperplasia and then necrosis of Peyer's patches in the second to third week can ulcerate into the bowel wall, causing intestinal bleeding or perforation.
Persistence in the gallbladder, especially with gallstones, creates chronic carriers who keep shedding in stool and sustain community transmission.
Plasmid- and chromosome-mediated resistance (gyrA mutations, ESBL-producing and extensively drug-resistant strains) drives treatment failure and makes culture-directed therapy essential.

symptoms: Fever lasting more than 3 days, often rising in a step-ladder pattern
Constipation in adults, or diarrhoea, which is more common in children
physicalSigns: Rose spots: faint salmon-coloured macules on the trunk, seen infrequently
Diffuse abdominal tenderness, sometimes in the right iliac fossa
Toxic, apathetic appearance in established disease
redFlags: Sudden severe abdominal pain, guarding, rigidity or loss of bowel sounds: suspect intestinal perforation and get an urgent surgical review
Melaena or fresh rectal bleeding (intestinal haemorrhage)
Altered sensorium, delirium or 'typhoid state' (encephalopathy)
Hypotension, shock or signs of septic shock
Chest pain, arrhythmia or heart failure suggesting myocarditis
Jaundice or rising bilirubin (typhoid hepatitis), or acute kidney injury
No clinical response after 5 days of appropriate therapy: look for a complication or a resistant isolate
Culture reports ceftriaxone-resistant or extensively drug-resistant (XDR) Salmonella: WHO AWaRe Watch/Reserve escalation needs infectious diseases approval

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Paroxysmal fever with rigors. Positive peripheral smear or bivalent rapid diagnostic test (RDT). Test for malaria in every febrile patient in endemic areas before attributing fever to enteric fever.
Abrupt high fever with retro-orbital pain, myalgia and rash. Leucopenia with falling platelets and rising haematocrit. Positive NS1 antigen in the first 5 days or IgM afterwards.
Painless black eschar, often in the groin, axilla or under clothing, with regional lymphadenopathy. Transaminitis. Positive IgM ELISA. Rapid defervescence on doxycycline.
Exposure to floodwater or animal urine. Conjunctival suffusion, calf tenderness, jaundice with acute kidney injury. Positive IgM ELISA or MAT.
Fever for weeks with weight loss and night sweats. Ascites or abdominal lymph nodes on ultrasound. Miliary chest X-ray. NAAT or culture evidence of M. tuberculosis.
Fever settles as jaundice appears. Transaminases often above 1,000 IU/L. Positive IgM anti-HAV or anti-HEV.
Right upper quadrant pain and point tenderness over the liver. Ultrasound shows a hypoechoic lesion.

ruleIn.testName: Blood culture: two sets before the first antibiotic dose
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Blood culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing for Salmonella Typhi / Paratyphi A
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Growth of S. Typhi or S. Paratyphi A, with a susceptibility profile covering ceftriaxone, azithromycin, ciprofloxacin, co-trimoxazole, chloramphenicol and, where relevant, meropenem
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: The reference test, most sensitive in the first week. ICMR 2019 requires two sets before empirical therapy. The susceptibility result drives step-down and de-escalation, which is the core AMR safeguard.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Bone marrow aspirate culture for Salmonella Typhi / Paratyphi A
ruleIn.targetCondition: Enteric fever with negative blood cultures or prior antibiotics
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Growth of S. Typhi or S. Paratyphi A
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Higher yield than blood culture and less affected by prior antibiotics. Reserve it for prolonged pyrexia of unknown origin where the result changes management.

ruleIn.testName: Complete blood count and liver function tests
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Haematology and biochemistry supportive of enteric fever
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Normal or low white cell count with relative eosinopenia. Mild thrombocytopenia. Moderately raised transaminases.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supportive pattern only, not diagnostic. Also the baseline for monitoring complications such as hepatitis and marrow suppression.

ruleOut.testName: Malaria microscopy or bivalent rapid diagnostic test
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Peripheral smear or Pf/Pv RDT for Plasmodium
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Negative smear/RDT supports a non-malarial cause; positive result redirects to the malaria pathway
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Mandatory for every febrile patient in endemic India before antibacterial therapy is committed.

ruleOut.testName: Dengue NS1 antigen (days 1–5) or IgM ELISA (from day 5)
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Dengue is co-endemic and needs a different fluid-led pathway with no antibiotic.

ruleOut.expectedFinding: Negative IgM in the right clinical window helps exclude scrub typhus
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Scrub typhus needs doxycycline (Access), not ceftriaxone. Missing it delays effective therapy and adds Watch-group exposure.

ruleOut.testName: Erect chest X-ray and abdominal ultrasound
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Imaging for perforation, abscess or alternative focus
ruleOut.targetCondition: Typhoid intestinal perforation, liver abscess or abdominal tuberculosis
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Free subdiaphragmatic gas indicates perforation. Ultrasound may show liver abscess, ascites or lymph nodes pointing to another diagnosis.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Use urgently when abdominal red flags are present. Perforation is a surgical emergency.

ruleOut.testName: Widal test (not to be used alone)
ruleOut.expectedFinding: A single raised titre is non-specific in endemic India. A negative result does not exclude enteric fever.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Listed so clinicians do not use it: a single Widal neither rules in nor rules out enteric fever, and it drives unnecessary antibiotic use. Do not start or stop antibiotics on Widal alone.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess severity and culture before antibiotics
actions: Triage with vital signs, hydration status, conscious level and abdominal examination for peritonism.
Draw two sets of blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose, as ICMR 2019 requires.
Send a malaria smear or RDT, dengue NS1/IgM and scrub typhus IgM as indicated by fever duration and exposure.
Send CBC, LFT, renal function and electrolytes.
Classify as uncomplicated (tolerating oral, no red flags) or complicated (cannot take oral, any red flag or toxic appearance).

branches.condition: Peritonism, free gas or suspected perforation
actions: Keep nil by mouth, insert IV access, resuscitate with IV fluids and call surgery urgently for laparotomy.
Start IV ceftriaxone after cultures and add anaerobic cover per surgical protocol. Record a planned stop date at the time of prescribing.

branches.condition: Shock, encephalopathy or major GI bleeding
actions: Resuscitate and escalate to HDU/ICU.
Start IV ceftriaxone after cultures. For gastrointestinal bleeding, cross-match blood and get a surgical/GI review.

clinicalManagement.title: Start empirical antibiotics by severity
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Within 1 hour of cultures in complicated disease; same visit in uncomplicated disease
actions: Uncomplicated adult: azithromycin 500 mg PO once daily (ICMR 2019, Table 2.2). WHO AWaRe WATCH antibiotic: confirm the diagnosis is plausible and cultures are sent before prescribing.
Uncomplicated child: azithromycin 20 mg/kg/day PO or cefixime 20 mg/kg/day PO (ICMR 2019, p. 11). Both are WHO AWaRe WATCH.
Complicated, or unable to take oral: ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily (adult; ICMR 2019, Table 2.2). WHO AWaRe WATCH antibiotic.
Complicated child: ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day IV, max 4 g/day (IAP 2022, Table 2). WHO AWaRe WATCH antibiotic.

Do NOT use ciprofloxacin or other fluoroquinolones empirically. ICMR 2019 reports S. Typhi quinolone resistance as high as 69%. Fluoroquinolones are WHO AWaRe WATCH and are used only when the isolate is proven susceptible.

Write the hard stop date on the chart at initiation. Adults: total course 10–14 days (ICMR 2019, p. 9), never more than 14 days. Children: at least 7 days after defervescence or 14 days total, whichever is later; azithromycin 7 days (IAP 2022).

branches.condition: History of penicillin anaphylaxis, angioedema or severe cutaneous reaction
actions: Uncomplicated: azithromycin (adult 500 mg once daily; child 20 mg/kg/day, max 1 g) (IAP 2022, Table 1).
Complicated: aztreonam (adult 1–2 g IV every 8 h; child 50–100 mg/kg/day, max 8 g). SEVERE AMR WARNING: WHO AWaRe RESERVE — notify the stewardship team.
Do not give ceftriaxone or cefixime: the product information lists penicillin hypersensitivity as a contraindication.

branches.condition: CKD or chronic liver disease
actions: Cefixime: 75% dose if CrCl 21–60 mL/min, 50% if 20 or below. Ceftriaxone: no change unless CrCl below 10 mL/min (max 2 g/day).
Azithromycin: no renal change; stop if hepatitis develops. Child with hepatitis needing IV therapy: cefotaxime preferred over ceftriaxone (IAP 2022).

clinicalManagement.title: Mandatory 48-hour review and culture-first de-escalation
actions: Reassess clinical status and chase culture and susceptibility results at 48 hours (ICMR 2019, p. 8).

Change the empirical regimen to match susceptibility (ICMR 2019, p. 9). Prefer the narrowest effective agent; WHO AWaRe ACCESS options such as co-trimoxazole or chloramphenicol are reasonable only if the isolate is susceptible.
Remember that defervescence on third-generation cephalosporins is slow (ICMR 2019, p. 8). Persistent fever alone in the first days is not a reason to escalate.

branches.condition: Culture positive and susceptible to an oral agent; patient afebrile, clinically improving and tolerating oral intake
actions: Step down from IV ceftriaxone to the oral agent the isolate is susceptible to.
Count IV days towards the total; the total course stays within 10–14 days.

branches.condition: Cultures negative and patient improving
actions: Continue the current agent to complete the course, stepping down to oral azithromycin when tolerated.
Re-examine the diagnosis if the clinical picture fits another pathway.

branches.condition: Not improving by day 5 of appropriate therapy
actions: Look for complications: ultrasound abdomen for abscess or perforation, and repeat cultures.
Review isolate resistance and get an infectious diseases opinion before changing antibiotic.

branches.condition: Culture shows ceftriaxone-resistant / ESBL or extensively drug-resistant (XDR) Salmonella
actions: SEVERE AMR WARNING: escalation to a carbapenem (meropenem, WHO AWaRe WATCH) is permitted only with a documented susceptibility result and infectious diseases / antimicrobial stewardship approval.
Combine with azithromycin only if the isolate is susceptible, and set the duration with the ID team.
Notify infection control and the hospital antibiogram team.
Never use WHO AWaRe RESERVE agents (for example colistin) for Salmonella.

clinicalManagement.title: Supportive care and complication monitoring
actions: Give paracetamol for fever. Avoid NSAIDs because of the intestinal bleeding and perforation risk.
Maintain hydration with oral rehydration, or IV fluids if not tolerating oral.
Examine the abdomen daily, especially in the second to third week, for perforation or bleeding.
Monitor CBC, LFT and renal function as clinically indicated.

clinicalManagement.title: Disposition and stop date
actions: Stop antibiotics on the documented stop date: adults 10–14 days total, never more than 14; children per IAP 2022 (at least 7 days after defervescence or 14 days, whichever is later).
Complete IDSP surveillance reporting for culture-confirmed enteric fever as local rules require.
Give the patient written advice to return urgently with abdominal pain, bleeding or recurrent fever (relapse).

patientEducation: Complete the prescribed course exactly and stop on the stated date; do not keep leftover antibiotics or buy more over the counter.
Relapse can occur 1–3 weeks after recovery: return for review with recurrent fever.
Return immediately with severe abdominal pain, black or bloody stools, confusion or fainting.
Wash hands with soap after using the toilet and before handling food.
A single Widal test does not prove or disprove typhoid; diagnosis rests on blood culture.
lifestyleAndDiet: Drink only boiled, chlorinated or packaged water during recovery and afterwards.
Eat soft, freshly cooked, easily digestible food. Avoid street food, raw salads and cut fruit from unknown sources.
Rest until fever-free and energy returns. Increase activity gradually.
Household members can receive typhoid conjugate vaccine (TCV) as per national immunisation guidance.
mdtReferrals: General surgery: urgent referral for suspected perforation or uncontrolled GI bleeding.
Infectious diseases / antimicrobial stewardship team: any Watch-to-carbapenem escalation, XDR isolate or treatment failure.
Infection prevention and control: XDR or ESBL isolates, and food-handler cases.
Public health / IDSP unit: culture-confirmed cases and clusters.
dischargeCriteria: Afebrile for at least 48 hours without antipyretics.
Tolerating oral diet, fluids and oral antibiotics.
No clinical evidence of perforation, bleeding or encephalopathy.
Oral step-down agent chosen from culture susceptibility where available, with the stop date written on the discharge summary.
Patient understands the warning signs for complications and relapse.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review in clinic or primary care 1 week after discharge and again at the end of therapy to confirm resolution and check that antibiotics stopped on the documented date. Check for relapse at 2–4 weeks if symptoms recur. Food handlers and healthcare workers need stool cultures to exclude chronic carriage before returning to work, per local public health rules.

regimens.duration: 7 days; total antibiotic course never above 14 days
adjustments: Paediatric: 20 mg/kg/day once daily, max 1 g/day, total 7 days (IAP 2022, Table 2).
Penicillin allergy: Preferred agent in penicillin allergy for outpatients (IAP 2022, Table 1).
CKD: No dose change (ICMR 2019 renal table not provided; azithromycin is mainly biliary-excreted). Use with caution if CrCl below 10 mL/min (product label).
CLD: No standard dose change; azithromycin can cause hepatotoxicity — check LFTs at baseline and stop if hepatitis develops (product label). Avoid in decompensated cirrhosis if an alternative exists.
AMR: WHO AWaRe WATCH. Prescribe only after blood cultures; IAP 2022 asks that azithromycin be kept as a reserve drug in children and justified by culture.
monitoring: QT if on other QT-prolonging drugs
contraindications: History of cholestatic jaundice with prior azithromycin
regimens.sourceTitle: ICMR Treatment Guidelines for Antimicrobial Use in Common Syndromes

adjustments: Paediatric: 20 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses, max 1,200 mg/day (IAP 2022, Table 2; twice-daily split is derived). Treat at least 7 days after defervescence or 14 days total, whichever is later (IAP 2022). IAP lists cefixime as first-line oral agent in children.
Penicillin allergy: Cephalosporin: do not use with a history of penicillin anaphylaxis, angioedema or severe cutaneous reaction; use azithromycin instead (IAP 2022, Table 1).
CKD: CrCl 21–60 mL/min or haemodialysis: 75% of standard dose (300 mg daily); CrCl 20 or below or peritoneal dialysis: 50% (200 mg daily) (cefixime label).
CLD: No dose change.
AMR: WHO AWaRe WATCH. Adult dose from cefixime product label (400 mg daily).
regimens.sourceTitle: IAP Standard Treatment Guidelines: Enteric Fever
regimens.useWhen: Child (IAP first-line) or azithromycin not tolerated / culture shows azithromycin non-susceptibility

regimens.duration: 10–14 days total including oral step-down (ICMR 2019, p. 9); never above 14 days in adults
adjustments: Paediatric: 100 mg/kg/day, max 4 g/day (IAP 2022, Table 2). Treat at least 7 days after defervescence or 14 days total, whichever is later (IAP 2022). Avoid in hyperbilirubinaemic neonates and never co-infuse with IV calcium in neonates (ceftriaxone label). IAP prefers cefotaxime 150–200 mg/kg/day (max 8 g) when hepatitis is present.
Penicillin allergy: Do not give with a history of penicillin hypersensitivity per product information; switch to the aztreonam row (IAP 2022, Table 1).
CKD: No dose change if liver function is normal; if CrCl is below 10 mL/min do not exceed 2 g daily; no supplemental dose after dialysis (ceftriaxone product information).
CLD: No dose change if renal function is normal; with combined severe renal and hepatic impairment, monitor plasma ceftriaxone levels (ceftriaxone product information).
AMR: WHO AWaRe WATCH. Step down to an oral agent matched to susceptibility once afebrile and tolerating oral; IV days count toward the total.
regimens.sourceTitle: ICMR Treatment Guidelines for Antimicrobial Use in Common Syndromes

regimens.indication: Complicated enteric fever with penicillin allergy
regimens.duration: Same total course as ceftriaxone; never above 14 days in adults
adjustments: Paediatric: 50–100 mg/kg/day, max 8 g/day (IAP 2022, Table 2), given in 3–4 divided doses (derived).
Penicillin allergy: Alternative for complicated disease in penicillin allergy (IAP 2022, Table 1). No cross-reactivity with penicillins; avoid only with a ceftazidime allergy (shared side chain).
CKD: Give the full loading dose, then reduce maintenance by half if CrCl 10–30 mL/min and to one quarter if below 10 mL/min (aztreonam label; not opened this session — confirm with pharmacy).
CLD: No dose change; monitor LFTs.

SEVERE AMR WARNING: WHO AWaRe RESERVE. Use only for a documented severe penicillin allergy, with stewardship notification. Adult dose from aztreonam label (not opened this session) — IAP gives the paediatric dose only.
regimens.sourceTitle: IAP Standard Treatment Guidelines: Enteric Fever
regimens.useWhen: History of penicillin anaphylaxis, angioedema or severe cutaneous reaction

regimens.duration: Duration set with infectious diseases; stop date documented at start
adjustments: Paediatric: 20 mg/kg every 8 h, max 1 g per dose (meropenem label; not opened this session). IAP 2022 permits meropenem only if the child is unstable or severely ill with a ceftriaxone-resistant isolate.

Penicillin allergy: Carbapenem cross-reactivity with penicillin is low (under 1%); with a history of penicillin anaphylaxis, give the first dose under observation or choose azithromycin if the isolate is susceptible and the patient is stable.
CKD: eGFR 26–50: standard dose every 12 h; 10–25: half dose every 12 h; below 10: half dose every 24 h (ULHT renal dosing guide 2018).
CLD: No dose change.
SEVERE AMR WARNING: WHO AWaRe WATCH (carbapenem). Requires a documented susceptibility result and ID/antimicrobial stewardship approval. Never use colistin (RESERVE) for Salmonella.
regimens.sourceTitle: IAP Standard Treatment Guidelines: Enteric Fever
regimens.useWhen: Isolate ceftriaxone-resistant and the patient unstable or severely ill

adjustments: Paediatric: 20 mg/kg/day once daily, max 1 g/day, 7 days (IAP 2022: drug of choice for ceftriaxone-resistant isolates in children).
Penicillin allergy: No beta-lactam in this regimen; a penicillin allergy does not change the choice.
CKD: No dose change (ICMR 2019 renal table not provided; azithromycin is mainly biliary-excreted). Use with caution if CrCl below 10 mL/min (product label).
CLD: No standard dose change; azithromycin can cause hepatotoxicity — check LFTs at baseline and stop if hepatitis develops (product label). Avoid in decompensated cirrhosis if an alternative exists.
AMR: WHO AWaRe WATCH. Use only when the isolate is azithromycin-susceptible.

title: Malaria (P. falciparum and P. vivax): Test-Confirmed Treatment and Severe Malaria (India)

pathophysiology.summary: Protozoal infection transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes. In India, Plasmodium falciparum and P. vivax cause almost all cases. Sporozoites mature in the liver, then merozoites invade red cells and cause cyclical haemolysis and fever. P. falciparum causes severe disease through cytoadherence and microvascular sequestration. P. vivax forms dormant liver hypnozoites that cause relapse. ICMR 2019 reports P. falciparum chloroquine resistance of at least 25% nationally, so artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) is first-line for falciparum.
keyMechanisms: Synchronous rupture of infected red cells releases pyrogens, causing paroxysmal fever with rigors and haemolytic anaemia.

P. falciparum-infected cells express PfEMP1 and adhere to endothelium in brain, kidney, lung and placenta. This causes microvascular obstruction, cerebral malaria, acute kidney injury, ARDS and lactic acidosis.
P. vivax hypnozoites persist in the liver and need a 14-day primaquine course for radical cure; primaquine causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
Hypoglycaemia comes from parasite glucose consumption, impaired gluconeogenesis and quinine-induced hyperinsulinaemia, especially in pregnancy.
Antimalarial drug resistance (chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum and emerging partner-drug resistance) is driven by presumptive treatment and artemisinin monotherapy.

symptoms: Fever, often with chills and rigors, which may be daily, tertian or irregular
Recent residence in or travel to an endemic district
redFlags: Impaired consciousness, convulsions or coma (cerebral malaria)
Prostration: unable to sit, stand or walk without help
Respiratory distress, acidotic breathing or pulmonary oedema
Shock or circulatory collapse (algid malaria)
Hypoglycaemia, especially in pregnancy or during quinine therapy
Severe anaemia, jaundice, haemoglobinuria (dark urine) or abnormal bleeding
Oliguria or rising creatinine (acute kidney injury)
Hyperparasitaemia on smear
Malaria in pregnancy: refer to hospital without delay (National Drug Policy on Malaria 2013)
Haematuria, dark urine or cyanosis on primaquine: stop primaquine immediately (G6PD-related haemolysis)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Retro-orbital pain, rash and severe myalgia. Rising haematocrit with leucopenia. Positive NS1/IgM. Negative malaria smear/RDT.
Gradual step-ladder fever, relative bradycardia, abdominal symptoms. Positive blood culture for Salmonella.
Eschar, lymphadenopathy, transaminitis. Positive IgM ELISA. Negative malaria tests.
Floodwater exposure, conjunctival suffusion, calf tenderness, combined jaundice and acute kidney injury.
Focal source or meningism. Positive blood or CSF culture. Malaria tests negative. Cerebral malaria and meningitis can coexist, so do a lumbar puncture when indicated.
Fever with encephalopathy and CSF pleocytosis. Negative malaria smear/RDT. JE IgM in CSF or serum.

ruleIn.testName: Peripheral blood smear microscopy (thick and thin films)
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Giemsa-stained microscopy for Plasmodium species and parasite density
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Asexual Plasmodium forms. Species identified (P. falciparum, P. vivax or mixed) and parasite density quantified.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: National Drug Policy 2013 requires confirmation by microscopy or RDT in every suspected case. Microscopy is used where results are available within 24 hours. Parasite density guides severity assessment and response monitoring.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Antigen detection (HRP2 / pLDH) for P. falciparum and P. vivax
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Used where microscopy is not available within 24 hours (NDP 2013) and by frontline workers (ASHAs) in high-burden areas. Enables test-before-treat and avoids presumptive treatment.

ruleIn.testName: Severity panel: capillary/plasma glucose, CBC, creatinine, bilirubin, lactate or venous gas
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Biochemistry and haematology for WHO severe malaria criteria
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Hypoglycaemia, severe anaemia, raised creatinine, raised bilirubin or acidosis/raised lactate meet severe criteria
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Any severe criterion moves the patient to the parenteral artesunate branch. Repeat glucose frequently, especially in pregnancy and with quinine.

ruleOut.expectedFinding: Normal activity permits the 14-day primaquine course; deficiency requires withholding or specialist-modified primaquine
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Primaquine is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency, pregnancy and infancy (NDP 2013). Test where available before the 14-day radical-cure course.

ruleOut.testName: Blood cultures (in severe malaria or shock)
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No growth supports stopping any empirical antibiotic
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Algid malaria and bacteraemia overlap. Culture first so any empirical WHO AWaRe Watch antibiotic can be stopped at 48 hours if negative.

ruleOut.testName: Dengue NS1/IgM and scrub typhus IgM
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Negative supports malaria as the sole cause
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Co-infections occur in India. Persistent fever after a parasitological response should prompt these tests.

ruleOut.testName: Lumbar puncture (when safe) in impaired consciousness
ruleOut.modalityTarget: CSF analysis for meningitis or encephalitis
ruleOut.expectedFinding: CSF is normal or near-normal in cerebral malaria. Pleocytosis or a positive Gram stain points to another diagnosis.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Cerebral malaria is a diagnosis of exclusion when malaria tests are positive but meningitis has not been excluded.

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm parasitologically and assess severity
actions: Confirm every suspected case by microscopy or RDT before treatment. Presumptive chloroquine is no longer recommended (NDP 2013), and ICMR 2019 advises treatment after confirmation only.
Check bedside glucose, vital signs, conscious level (GCS) and urine output.
Identify species (Pf, Pv or mixed), pregnancy status and the state of residence: north-eastern states use ACT-AL, other states ACT-SP.

Screen against WHO severe malaria criteria: impaired consciousness, prostration, convulsions, acidosis, hypoglycaemia, severe anaemia, AKI, jaundice, pulmonary oedema, significant bleeding, shock or hyperparasitaemia.

branches.condition: Any severe criterion present, or unable to take oral medication
actions: Go to the severe malaria step immediately.
Refer or transfer to a facility with inpatient and critical care capability (NDP 2013).

branches.condition: Uncomplicated and test-confirmed
actions: Start the species- and region-specific oral regimen in the next step.

branches.condition: Neither microscopy nor RDT available
actions: Give a full course of chloroquine while microscopy results are awaited (NDP 2013), then switch to the confirmed-species regimen.
Do not give artemisinin monotherapy.

clinicalManagement.title: Uncomplicated malaria: species- and region-specific oral therapy
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Start the same visit as confirmation
actions: Give doses under direct observation where possible, and give oral doses with food.

branches.condition: P. vivax (not pregnant)
actions: Chloroquine 25 mg/kg total over 3 days: 10 mg/kg on day 1, 10 mg/kg on day 2, 5 mg/kg on day 3 (NDP 2013).
Radical cure: primaquine 0.25 mg/kg daily for 14 days, given under supervision, only if G6PD is not deficient (NDP 2013).
Primaquine is contraindicated in pregnancy, infants and G6PD deficiency. Stop it immediately if dark or red urine or cyanosis develops.

branches.condition: P. falciparum, states other than the north-east (not first trimester)
actions: ACT-SP: artesunate 4 mg/kg once daily for 3 days, plus sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine 25 mg/kg sulfadoxine + 1.25 mg/kg pyrimethamine on day 1 only (NDP 2013).
Gametocytocidal primaquine 0.75 mg/kg single dose on day 2 (NDP 2013), except in pregnancy and infants.
SP is not for children under 5 months; use another ACT for them.

branches.condition: P. falciparum, north-eastern states (not first trimester)
actions: ACT-AL: artemether-lumefantrine twice daily for 3 days by weight band. Adults over 34 kg: 80/480 mg (4 tablets of 20/120 mg) per dose (NDP 2013).
Primaquine 0.75 mg/kg single dose on day 2 (NDP 2013), except in pregnancy and infants.

branches.condition: Mixed P. falciparum + P. vivax infection
actions: Region-specific ACT for 3 days (ACT-AL in the north-east, ACT-SP elsewhere), plus primaquine 0.25 mg/kg daily for 14 days if G6PD is not deficient (NDP 2013).

branches.condition: Pregnancy with uncomplicated P. falciparum
actions: First trimester: quinine salt 10 mg/kg three times daily for 7 days (NDP 2013); monitor for hypoglycaemia.
Second and third trimesters: region-specific ACT.
Never give primaquine in pregnancy. Refer to hospital without delay.

clinicalManagement.title: Severe malaria: parenteral artesunate and critical care
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Within the first hour of recognition
actions: Artesunate 2.4 mg/kg IV or IM at 0, 12 and 24 hours, then once daily (NDP 2013; ICMR 2019 p. 16). Children under 20 kg: 3 mg/kg per dose (ICMR 2019). Parenteral artesunate is the treatment of choice for all severe malaria.
Continue parenteral therapy for at least 24 hours and until the patient can tolerate oral medication, then give a full 3-day course of region-specific oral ACT (NDP 2013).

If artesunate is unavailable: artemether 3.2 mg/kg IM on admission, then 1.6 mg/kg daily; or quinine 20 mg/kg salt loading dose (omit if quinine already given), then 10 mg/kg every 8 hours, infusion rate not exceeding 5 mg/kg/hour (NDP 2013).
Check glucose at least every 4 hours (hourly if unconscious) and treat hypoglycaemia with IV dextrose.
Use conservative IV fluids to avoid pulmonary oedema. Do not give corticosteroids, mannitol, heparin or adrenaline (NDP 2013).
Escalate to ICU for coma, shock, respiratory failure or AKI needing dialysis.

branches.condition: Shock (algid malaria) or suspected bacterial co-infection
actions: Take blood cultures first, then add empirical ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily. WHO AWaRe WATCH antibiotic.
Mandatory 48-hour antibiotic review: stop if cultures are negative and no bacterial focus is found; otherwise de-escalate to the narrowest agent by susceptibility.
Write a hard stop date at initiation.

branches.condition: Quinine used as the parenteral agent
actions: Complete with oral quinine 10 mg/kg three times daily for 7 days plus doxycycline 3 mg/kg daily for 7 days, or clindamycin 10 mg/kg twice daily for 7 days in pregnancy and children under 8 (NDP 2013). Doxycycline and clindamycin are WHO AWaRe ACCESS; the 7-day cap is fixed.
Monitor glucose and the QT interval.

clinicalManagement.title: Monitor treatment response
actions: Repeat smear microscopy in severe malaria to document falling parasitaemia.
If fever persists after 72 hours of ACT, repeat microscopy to look for treatment failure and test for co-infection (dengue, scrub typhus, enteric fever).
Watch for post-artesunate delayed haemolysis: check haemoglobin in the weeks after severe malaria.
Do not start antibacterials for persistent fever without a microbiological or clinical focus.

clinicalManagement.title: Notify and plan disposition
actions: Report every confirmed case to the NCVBDC / IDSP surveillance system per state rules.
Confirm the full ACT or chloroquine course and the primaquine supply, with supervision arranged for the 14-day course.

patientEducation: Take the full course even when you feel better. Stopping early causes relapse and drives drug resistance.
For P. vivax: the 14-day primaquine course prevents the infection returning from the liver. Stop and return immediately if urine turns dark, red or black, or lips turn blue.
Do not buy single-drug artemisinin tablets from a pharmacy; they promote resistance.
Any future fever needs a malaria test (smear or RDT) before treatment.
Pregnant women with fever must go to a health facility the same day.
lifestyleAndDiet: Sleep under a long-lasting insecticidal net (LLIN) every night.
Remove standing water around the home and allow indoor residual spraying.
Wear long sleeves and use repellents at dusk and dawn.
Eat normally with adequate fluids during recovery. Iron-rich foods help recovery from anaemia.
mdtReferrals: Critical care: cerebral malaria, shock, ARDS or AKI.
Nephrology: AKI needing renal replacement therapy.
Obstetrics: any malaria in pregnancy.
District malaria officer / NCVBDC: case notification, contact and focal vector control.
Antimicrobial stewardship team: any empirical antibiotic beyond the 48-hour review.
dischargeCriteria: Afebrile for at least 24–48 hours with a documented parasitological response on smear.
Tolerating and completing the oral ACT or chloroquine course.
No hypoglycaemia, stable haemoglobin and recovering renal function.
Primaquine supply and supervision arranged where indicated, after a G6PD check.
Case notified to the surveillance system.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review at the end of the 3-day oral course. For P. vivax, review at completion of the 14-day primaquine course (with a haemoglobin check if haemolysis is a concern). After severe malaria treated with artesunate, check haemoglobin at about 1–4 weeks for delayed haemolysis. Re-test immediately with any recurrence of fever, especially within 28 days (possible recrudescence) or months later with P. vivax (relapse).

title: Pulmonary Tuberculosis (Drug-Sensitive): NAAT-Led Diagnosis and NTEP Treatment (India)

pathophysiology.summary: Chronic granulomatous infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, transmitted by airborne droplet nuclei from people with infectious pulmonary disease. Most infections are contained as latent TB. Progression to active disease follows immune compromise, with HIV, diabetes, undernutrition, smoking and alcohol use the main drivers in India. The National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP) treats drug-sensitive TB with daily weight-band fixed-dose combinations (2HRZE/4HRE). Every patient is tested upfront for rifampicin resistance.
keyMechanisms: Inhaled bacilli are taken up by alveolar macrophages and survive inside them. Cell-mediated immunity forms caseating granulomas that contain but do not always eradicate infection.
Reactivation with caseous necrosis and liquefaction creates cavities with a very high bacillary load, which drives infectiousness and the selection of resistant mutants.
Erosion of cavity walls into vessels causes haemoptysis, which can be massive (Rasmussen aneurysm).
Haematogenous spread causes miliary, meningeal, skeletal and other extrapulmonary disease.
Monotherapy, irregular adherence or empirical fluoroquinolone use selects rpoB, katG/inhA and gyrA mutants (rifampicin-, isoniazid- and fluoroquinolone-resistant TB).

symptoms: Unintentional weight loss and loss of appetite
physicalSigns: Low body mass index or wasting
Crackles or bronchial breathing over upper zones
Signs of pleural effusion (dullness, reduced breath sounds)
redFlags: Massive haemoptysis or haemodynamic instability
Respiratory failure, hypoxaemia or tension pneumothorax
Headache, neck stiffness, altered sensorium or cranial nerve palsy: suspect TB meningitis
Back pain with leg weakness or sphincter disturbance (spinal TB with cord compression)
Pericardial effusion or tamponade
Jaundice, vomiting or abdominal pain on treatment (drug-induced hepatitis): stop hepatotoxic drugs and review the same day
Rifampicin resistance detected on NAAT: refer to the nodal DR-TB centre; do not start a first-line regimen
Empirical fluoroquinolone already given for 'pneumonia' before TB testing: SEVERE AMR WARNING, risk of masked TB and fluoroquinolone resistance

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Acute onset over days, lobar consolidation, response to a 5-day antibiotic course (ICMR 2019). Consider TB when the illness is protracted (ICMR 2019, p. 38).
Older smoker, mass lesion or hilar lymphadenopathy, NAAT negative. Diagnosis by CT and tissue biopsy.
AFB smear positive but NAAT negative for M. tuberculosis. Speciation on culture.
Pre-existing cavity (often post-TB), fungal ball on CT, positive Aspergillus IgG. Often misdiagnosed as TB relapse.
Chronic daily purulent sputum, dilated airways on HRCT, NAAT negative.
Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, non-caseating granulomas, negative mycobacterial tests.

ruleIn.testName: Nucleic acid amplification test (CBNAAT/Truenat) on sputum
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Molecular detection of M. tuberculosis complex and rifampicin resistance
ruleIn.expectedFinding: MTB detected. Rifampicin resistance reported as not detected or detected.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Upfront NAAT for all presumptive TB under NTEP gives diagnosis and rifampicin resistance together. This is the culture-first equivalent for TB: the result decides first-line versus DR-TB pathway before any drug is started.

ruleIn.testName: First-line and second-line line probe assay (LPA) / culture-DST
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Universal drug susceptibility testing for isoniazid and fluoroquinolone resistance
ruleIn.expectedFinding: katG/inhA mutations (isoniazid resistance) or gyrA/gyrB mutations (fluoroquinolone resistance)
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Universal DST under NTEP. Isoniazid resistance changes the regimen. Fluoroquinolone resistance determines the DR-TB regimen.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Upper-zone infiltrates, cavitation, miliary nodules, hilar lymphadenopathy or pleural effusion
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports diagnosis and triage, especially when sputum is scanty. Never a substitute for microbiological confirmation.

ruleOut.testName: HIV test and blood glucose / HbA1c
ruleOut.modalityTarget: Comorbidity screening in every TB patient
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Results guide antiretroviral therapy, cotrimoxazole prophylaxis and glycaemic management
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: NTEP screens every TB patient for HIV and diabetes because both change treatment, monitoring and outcomes.

ruleOut.modalityTarget: ALT, AST and bilirubin before ATT
ruleOut.targetCondition: Pre-existing liver disease and risk of drug-induced liver injury
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Normal baseline; abnormal values need closer monitoring
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide are hepatotoxic. A baseline is needed to interpret later rises.

ruleOut.targetCondition: Lung cancer, bronchiectasis, aspergilloma or NTM disease
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Mass, dilated airways or fungal ball point to an alternative diagnosis
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Use when NAAT is negative but suspicion remains, or the X-ray is atypical.

ruleOut.expectedFinding: Growth of NTM rather than M. tuberculosis complex
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Separates NTM from TB when smear and NAAT disagree.

clinicalManagement.title: Identify presumptive TB and test before treating
actions: Treat cough for 2 weeks or more, fever, night sweats, weight loss or haemoptysis as presumptive TB.
Collect sputum for NAAT (CBNAAT/Truenat) before any antibiotic course.

Do not prescribe empirical fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, ciprofloxacin) for chest infection until TB is excluded. SEVERE AMR WARNING: these are WHO AWaRe WATCH, partially treat TB, delay diagnosis and select fluoroquinolone resistance that compromises DR-TB regimens.
Do not prescribe rifampicin as monotherapy for any other infection where TB is endemic (ICMR 2019, p. 27).
Record weight, BMI, HIV status and diabetes status, and check baseline LFTs.

branches.condition: Massive haemoptysis, respiratory failure or suspected TB meningitis
actions: Resuscitate and admit.
Arrange urgent respiratory, critical care or neurology input. For TB meningitis follow the NTEP extended regimen with corticosteroids.

branches.condition: NAAT: MTB detected, rifampicin resistance NOT detected
actions: Start the drug-sensitive regimen.
Send a sample for first-line LPA to check for isoniazid resistance (universal DST).

branches.condition: NAAT: MTB detected, rifampicin resistance DETECTED
actions: Refer to the nodal DR-TB centre the same week and send second-line LPA.
Do not start a first-line regimen. Treatment follows current NTEP programmatic management of DR-TB guidelines.
Linezolid used in DR-TB regimens is WHO AWaRe RESERVE: use only within the programme regimen.

branches.condition: NAAT negative but clinical/radiological suspicion persists
actions: Repeat NAAT, send culture and get a chest physician opinion before any empirical decision.

clinicalManagement.title: Notify and enrol
actions: Notify every diagnosed TB case on Ni-kshay; this is mandatory for public and private providers.
Enrol the patient for Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana nutritional direct benefit transfer.
Identify household contacts for screening and TB preventive treatment per NTEP.

clinicalManagement.title: Drug-sensitive TB regimen (2HRZE/4HRE)
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Intensive phase 8 weeks; continuation phase 16 weeks
actions: Intensive phase: 8 weeks (56 doses) of daily isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol as an FDC (H 75 mg / R 150 mg / Z 400 mg / E 275 mg).
Continuation phase: 16 weeks (112 doses) of daily isoniazid, rifampicin and ethambutol as an FDC (H 75 mg / R 150 mg / E 275 mg).
Adult weight bands, tablets per day in both phases: 25–34 kg = 2; 35–49 kg = 3; 50–64 kg = 4; 65–75 kg = 5; over 75 kg = 6.
Move to the next band if weight rises by more than 5 kg and crosses a band boundary.
Give pyridoxine 10 mg daily.
Support adherence with treatment supporter or digital adherence technology, recording doses on Ni-kshay.

branches.condition: CNS or skeletal TB
actions: Extend the continuation phase to 24 weeks.
For adult TB meningitis: give RHZE for 2 months, then RHE for at least 10 months, with dexamethasone 0.4 mg/kg/day IV tapered over 8–12 weeks.

branches.condition: Children (under 39 kg)
actions: Use the NTEP paediatric dispersible FDC weight bands (HRZ 50/75/150 mg, HR 50/75 mg, plus ethambutol 100 mg).
Manage with a paediatrician.

branches.condition: Isoniazid resistance on LPA, rifampicin susceptible
actions: Switch to the NTEP isoniazid-resistant regimen (levofloxacin added to rifampicin, ethambutol and pyrazinamide) after confirming fluoroquinolone susceptibility on second-line LPA.
Levofloxacin is used here only as a programme TB drug. Do not prescribe it outside this regimen.

clinicalManagement.title: Monitor toxicity and response
actions: Review monthly for adherence, weight (adjust the weight band), symptoms and adverse events.
Repeat sputum microscopy at the end of the intensive phase and at the end of treatment.
Ask about visual acuity and colour vision at each visit (ethambutol).

branches.condition: Jaundice, or ALT at least 3 times the upper limit with symptoms, or at least 5 times without symptoms
actions: Stop isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide and check LFTs.
Refer for physician review and reintroduce drugs sequentially per NTEP once LFTs recover.

branches.condition: Reduced visual acuity or colour vision
actions: Stop ethambutol and refer to ophthalmology.

patientEducation: TB is curable when every dose is taken daily for the full course. Missed doses cause drug-resistant TB that is much harder to treat.
Cover your mouth when coughing and ventilate rooms well; most patients stop being infectious within weeks of effective treatment.
Urine and tears may turn orange-red because of rifampicin; this is harmless.
Stop the tablets and come the same day with yellow eyes, vomiting, abdominal pain or blurred vision.
Do not take antibiotics such as levofloxacin or moxifloxacin from a pharmacy for cough; they mask TB and cause resistance.
Rifampicin reduces the effect of hormonal contraceptives; use a barrier or alternative method.
lifestyleAndDiet: Eat a high-calorie, high-protein diet. Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana provides monthly nutritional support by direct benefit transfer.
Stop smoking and avoid alcohol, which increases liver toxicity and treatment failure.
Keep blood glucose controlled if diabetic.
Sleep in a well-ventilated room, separately from young children if possible during the first weeks.
mdtReferrals: Nodal DR-TB centre: any rifampicin resistance or treatment failure.
ART centre: HIV co-infection.
Endocrinology / diabetes clinic: TB-diabetes.
Nutrition / dietetics: BMI under 18.5 or ongoing weight loss.
Ophthalmology: visual symptoms on ethambutol.
NTEP treatment supervisor / TB health visitor: adherence support and contact tracing.
dischargeCriteria: Clinically stable, with haemoptysis and respiratory failure resolved.
Tolerating the FDC regimen without hepatotoxicity.
Case notified on Ni-kshay with a treatment supporter and DOT/adherence plan in place.
Drug supply arranged until the next follow-up visit.
Household contact screening initiated.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Monthly clinical review with weight check and band adjustment throughout treatment. Sputum microscopy at the end of the intensive phase and at the end of treatment. After successful completion, NTEP post-treatment follow-up every 6 months for 2 years to detect recurrence early.

title: Scrub Typhus: Recognition, Doxycycline-First Treatment and Severe Disease (India)

pathophysiology.summary: Acute febrile illness caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi, an obligate intracellular bacterium transmitted by the bite of larval trombiculid mites (chiggers) in scrub vegetation, fields and peridomestic areas. It is a leading cause of acute undifferentiated febrile illness in India, peaking in the monsoon and post-monsoon months. Infection of endothelial cells causes disseminated vasculitis. Untreated, it can progress to multi-organ dysfunction, but it responds rapidly to doxycycline, a WHO AWaRe Access antibiotic.
keyMechanisms: Inoculation at the chigger bite site causes local necrosis that evolves into a painless black eschar, often in hidden moist areas such as the groin, axilla or under the waistband or breast.
Orientia infects endothelial cells and macrophages, causing systemic vasculitis and perivasculitis with increased vascular permeability.
Vascular leak and inflammation cause interstitial pneumonitis/ARDS, myocarditis, meningoencephalitis, hepatitis and acute kidney injury.

The organism is intracellular and lacks peptidoglycan, so beta-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems) are ineffective. Inappropriate ceftriaxone or meropenem adds AMR pressure and delays cure.
Rifampicin is active but monotherapy is discouraged in TB-endemic India because it selects rifampicin-resistant M. tuberculosis (ICMR 2019, p. 27).

symptoms: Acute fever, often high, for 5–14 days
Recent outdoor, agricultural or scrubland exposure
physicalSigns: Eschar: painless, punched-out black crust with an erythematous rim; examine the groin, axilla, genitalia, inframammary area and waistline
redFlags: Hypoxaemia, tachypnoea or bilateral infiltrates (ARDS / interstitial pneumonitis)
Hypotension or shock
Altered sensorium, seizures or neck stiffness (meningoencephalitis)
Oliguria or rising creatinine (AKI)
Jaundice or marked transaminitis
Myocarditis: arrhythmia, chest pain or heart failure
Any organ dysfunction: treat as severe scrub typhus with IV therapy and admit to HDU/ICU
Patient already on a cephalosporin or carbapenem without improvement: SEVERE AMR WARNING, these agents do not treat Orientia; add doxycycline and stop the beta-lactam if no other indication

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: No eschar. Haemoconcentration with leucopenia. Positive NS1/IgM. No response needed to doxycycline.
Positive smear or RDT. Paroxysmal rigors. No eschar.

Floodwater or animal-urine exposure, calf tenderness, conjunctival suffusion, prominent jaundice with AKI, positive Leptospira IgM/MAT. Doxycycline also covers it, but severe leptospirosis needs IV penicillin or ceftriaxone.
Gradual fever, relative bradycardia, abdominal symptoms, no eschar. Positive blood culture for Salmonella.

differentials.condition: Spotted fever group rickettsioses (Indian tick typhus)
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Prominent rash involving palms and soles, tick exposure. Same doxycycline treatment; confirm with specific serology.

differentials.condition: Japanese encephalitis or acute encephalitis syndrome
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Encephalopathy without eschar. CSF pleocytosis with JE IgM. In scrub-typhus-endemic AES belts, test for and treat scrub typhus as well.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: IgM optical density above the laboratory-validated regional cut-off, usually positive from the end of the first week of illness
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Main confirmatory test in Indian practice. May be negative early, so do not withhold doxycycline in a compatible case while results are pending.

ruleIn.testName: PCR on eschar swab/crust or blood buffy coat
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Molecular detection of O. tsutsugamushi DNA (for example 47-kDa or 56-kDa gene targets)
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Most useful in the first week before IgM appears. An eschar sample gives the highest yield.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Thrombocytopenia, raised transaminases, hypoalbuminaemia, raised creatinine in severe disease
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supportive pattern. Organ dysfunction defines the severe IV-therapy branch.

ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Required in every acute febrile illness in endemic India. Co-infection is possible.

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Serology for co-endemic acute febrile illnesses
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Negative supports scrub typhus as the sole diagnosis
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: These share the season and presentation. Dengue needs a no-antibiotic fluid pathway.

ruleOut.testName: Blood cultures (in severe disease or shock)
ruleOut.expectedFinding: No growth supports stopping any empirical beta-lactam at 48 hours
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Culture-first: lets any empirical Watch-group antibiotic be de-escalated or stopped.

ruleOut.expectedFinding: Bilateral interstitial infiltrates in scrub pneumonitis. Lobar consolidation suggests bacterial pneumonia.
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Defines respiratory severity and separates scrub pneumonitis from bacterial CAP.

ruleOut.testName: Weil-Felix test (not to be used alone)
ruleOut.expectedFinding: A negative result does not exclude scrub typhus
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Listed so it is not relied on: sensitivity is poor. Do not withhold doxycycline because of a negative Weil-Felix test.

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise, search for eschar and stratify severity
actions: Examine the whole skin, including the groin, axilla, genitalia, inframammary folds and waistline, for an eschar.
Send a malaria test, dengue NS1/IgM, scrub typhus IgM (or PCR in week 1), CBC, LFT, renal function and, if severe, blood cultures.
Classify as non-severe (no organ dysfunction, tolerating oral) or severe (any organ dysfunction: respiratory, cardiovascular, CNS, renal or hepatic).
Start treatment on clinical suspicion. Empirical doxycycline is appropriate when diagnostic facilities are unavailable (ICMR 2019, p. 27).

branches.condition: Organ dysfunction present
actions: Admit to HDU/ICU and go to the severe-disease step.

branches.condition: No organ dysfunction, tolerating oral
actions: Start oral doxycycline. Outpatient management is possible with review at 48 hours.

clinicalManagement.title: Non-severe scrub typhus: oral therapy
actions: Write a hard stop date at initiation: the standard course is 7 days (ICMR 2019, Table 2.7) and must never exceed 15 days.

branches.condition: Adult, not pregnant
actions: Doxycycline 100 mg PO twice daily for 7 days (ICMR 2019, Table 2.7). WHO AWaRe ACCESS: the preferred agent.
Take with a full glass of water, sitting upright, to avoid oesophageal ulceration.

branches.condition: Child under 45.5 kg
actions: Doxycycline 2.2 mg/kg PO twice daily for 7 days (ICMR 2019, Table 2.7).

branches.condition: Pregnancy or doxycycline intolerance
actions: Azithromycin 500 mg PO once daily (ICMR 2019, Table 2.2), with the course length capped and agreed with obstetrics/ID.
WHO AWaRe WATCH antibiotic: use only where doxycycline is contraindicated or not tolerated.

clinicalManagement.title: Severe scrub typhus: combination IV therapy
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Within 1 hour of recognising organ dysfunction
actions: Give IV doxycycline 100 mg twice daily plus IV azithromycin 500 mg once daily for 7 days. In the INTREST trial (Varghese et al., NEJM 2023; 794 patients across 7 Indian centres), combination IV therapy reduced the composite of death, persistent complications and persistent fever compared with either drug alone (33% vs 47% and 48%).
Azithromycin is WHO AWaRe WATCH. The 7-day course is a hard cap; switch IV to oral once the patient is afebrile and tolerating oral, without extending the total.
Give organ support as needed: oxygen or ventilation for ARDS, cautious fluids and vasopressors for shock, renal replacement therapy for AKI.

branches.condition: Empirical ceftriaxone or meropenem started for undifferentiated sepsis
actions: SEVERE AMR WARNING: beta-lactams do not treat Orientia.
Review at 48 hours with blood culture results. Stop the beta-lactam if cultures are negative and there is no other bacterial focus.
Meropenem is WHO AWaRe WATCH and must not continue without a documented culture indication.

branches.condition: Pregnancy
actions: Use IV azithromycin alone and avoid doxycycline.
Agree management jointly with obstetrics and infectious diseases.

clinicalManagement.title: 48-hour response review
actions: Expect defervescence within about 48 hours of doxycycline. This rapid response supports the diagnosis.
Review serology/PCR and culture results.

branches.condition: Afebrile and improving
actions: Complete 7 days in total and stop on the documented date.

branches.condition: Still febrile at 72 hours on doxycycline
actions: Re-examine the diagnosis and look for co-infection (malaria, dengue, leptospirosis, enteric fever) or complications.
Get an infectious diseases review.
Do not use rifampicin monotherapy (ICMR 2019, p. 27) or add broad-spectrum Watch agents without a microbiological indication.

patientEducation: Scrub typhus spreads through tiny mite bites in grass, bushes and fields, not from person to person.
Take the full 7-day course and stop on the stated date; fever usually settles within 2 days.
Take doxycycline with plenty of water and stay upright for 30 minutes. Avoid taking it at the same time as milk, antacids or iron.
Return urgently with breathlessness, confusion, reduced urine output or yellow eyes.
With future fevers after field exposure, tell the doctor and point out any black scab-like spot on the skin.
lifestyleAndDiet: Wear long trousers tucked into socks, long sleeves and closed footwear when working in fields or scrub.
Use insect repellent on skin and clothing during outdoor work.
Bathe and wash clothes after field work. Do not sit or lie directly on grass.
Eat a normal diet with good fluid intake during recovery.
mdtReferrals: Critical care: ARDS, shock or meningoencephalitis.
Nephrology: AKI needing renal replacement therapy.
Obstetrics: scrub typhus in pregnancy.
Infectious diseases / antimicrobial stewardship team: non-response at 72 hours or any beta-lactam continued beyond 48 hours.
District surveillance / IDSP unit: clusters of acute febrile illness or acute encephalitis syndrome.
dischargeCriteria: Afebrile for at least 24–48 hours.
Organ dysfunction resolving: off oxygen, haemodynamically stable, creatinine improving.
Tolerating oral doxycycline (or azithromycin in pregnancy), with the total course capped at 7 days and the stop date written on the discharge summary.
Any empirical beta-lactam stopped or justified by culture.
Patient understands the warning signs and prevention measures.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review at the end of the 7-day course to confirm resolution. After severe disease, recheck renal and liver function and chest status at 1–2 weeks. Re-present immediately with recurrent fever, breathlessness or neurological symptoms.

adjustments: Paediatric: Under 45.5 kg: 2.2 mg/kg every 12 h for 7 days (ICMR 2019, Table 2.7). Sources differ on age: ICMR 2019 gives this dose for rickettsial infection with no age floor; NDP 2013 contraindicates doxycycline under 8 years in the malaria context.
Penicillin allergy: No beta-lactam in this regimen; a penicillin allergy does not change the choice.
CKD: No dose change (ULHT renal dosing guide 2018: unchanged at eGFR 20–50, 10–20 and below 10).
CLD: No standard dose change; use with caution and avoid other hepatotoxic drugs where possible.
AMR: WHO AWaRe ACCESS — preferred agent.
